implementation_notes: Swift's profiling tools are Instruments (Time Profiler, Allocations, System Trace) and on Linux the perf-based tools; for micro-optimisation the specific costs to look for are retain/release traffic (measured by Instruments' Allocations, which shows ARC traffic that is invisible on the CPU profile), bridging between Swift and Objective-C (a bridging header call crosses the boundary and cannot be optimised), and existential/protocol dispatch (a call through a protocol witness table is an indirect call, the Swift analogue of devirtualisation). Swift's ARC is the usual measured cost: a tight loop retaining and releasing objects can spend more time in the retain-release path than in the work, and the fix is usually an unowned/unsafe pointer, a value type, or reusing a buffer. Release-only: Swift's optimiser (SILGen) makes different decisions in debug, so every measurement is a release build.
idiom_name: Instruments Time Profiler / Allocations attribution, then one targeted change at the measured hotspot; ARC traffic and bridging are the usual Swift costs
pitfalls: ARC retain/release traffic dominates a Swift hot loop and is invisible on the CPU profile - the Allocations template shows it, and a value type (struct) removes it entirely.
Existential dispatch (any P, a protocol-typed variable) is an indirect, boxed call the optimiser cannot resolve; a generic over a concrete type is specialised and inlinable.
Bridging to Objective-C on a hot path is not optimisable across the language boundary; keep the hot path in pure Swift.
Debug and release builds make different optimiser decisions, so a debug measurement is meaningless for this pattern.
Instruments itself has overhead; a long profiling session changes what is slow, so profile in pieces.
